pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9; polar food chains — Antarctic: phytoplankton → krill → fish & penguins → leopard seals & orcas; Arctic: algae under the ice → zooplankton → fish → seals → polar bears. Tiny organisms (krill, plankton) are the foundation that all polar life depends on.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (construct and interpret food chains; identify producers, predators and prey).
• Standards—US: NGSS 5-LS2-1 (movement of matter among organisms/environment; food webs); 3-LS4-3; MS-LS2-3 later.
• Operational details: teach the arrow as 'energy/food flows TO' (eaten-by), a common reversal error. Start every polar chain at a PRODUCER powered by sunlight (phytoplankton/ice algae), then follow the energy up through krill/zooplankton to top predators. The big idea: the smallest organisms (krill, plankton) support the largest animals — remove them and the whole chain collapses. Compare the two poles' parallel chains.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (7) put a simple polar chain in order from plankton to predator; Tier B (8) point the arrows the right way (eaten-by) and name the producer; Tier C (9) predict what happens up the chain if krill or plankton disappear.
bestPractices: Define the arrow explicitly as 'is eaten by / energy flows to' and rehearse it, because reversing it is the classic error
Always begin at a sunlight-powered producer (phytoplankton, ice algae) so the energy source is clear
Make krill/plankton the star: tiny animals holding up whales, penguins and seals — vivid and central to polar ecology
Run a remove-a-link prediction (take out krill) to reveal dependency and consequences up the chain
Compare Arctic and Antarctic chains side by side to show the same producer→consumer→predator pattern in both
keyRepresentations: Antarctic chain strip: phytoplankton → krill → penguin/fish → leopard seal/orca
Arctic chain strip: ice algae → zooplankton → fish → seal → polar bear
Arrow key showing direction = 'is eaten by / energy flows to'
Pyramid of numbers hinting many tiny krill support few big predators
commonMisconceptions: The arrow points from predator to prey — it points from the eaten to the eater (energy flows up)
Big animals are the most important — the tiny producers and krill actually support everything above them
Food chains start with an animal — they start with a producer powered by sunlight (plankton/algae)
Removing one small link doesn't matter — losing krill or plankton can collapse the whole chain
Arctic and Antarctic have totally different food systems — both follow the same producer→consumer→predator pattern

learn.summary: Children aged 7–9 build and reason about polar food chains. Antarctic: phytoplankton → krill → fish/penguins → leopard seals/orcas; Arctic: ice algae → zooplankton → fish → seals → polar bears. Core ideas: every chain begins at a sunlight-powered producer; the arrow means 'is eaten by / energy flows to' (points toward the eater); tiny organisms (plankton, krill) are the load-bearing base; and removing a small link ripples up to the biggest predators. The primary activity is constructing a chain and perturbing it; order/arrow-direction checks and a conversational hook are companions or scaffolds with narrower purposes.

activities.title: Build a polar chain and pull out the krill
feedback: If a learner reads 'krill → penguin' as 'krill eats penguin', re-state the arrow rule — it means 'is eaten by', pointing toward the eater — and re-read the whole chain aloud with that rule.
If a learner says only the krill is affected when krill are removed, prompt: fewer krill leads to fewer penguins, which leads to fewer leopard seals; have them walk the ripple up one step at a time.
If a learner names the leopard seal or orca as most important because it is biggest, ask what that animal depends on for food, and trace back down through penguins to krill and plankton.
If the chain is started with an animal, ask what powers the very first organism, and guide them to place a sunlight-powered producer (phytoplankton or ice algae) at the base.
activities.rationale: Constructing the chain and then perturbing it is intended to make energy flow and dependency feel causal rather than a memorised list, and directly rehearses the two documented errors (reversed arrows; undervaluing the base). An interactive builder where arrows lock to 'eaten by', bounce back when reversed, and a meter drops when krill are pulled out is one way to make the remove-a-link cascade visible; equally, physical cards with drawn arrows let children stage the same removal by hand. Comparative efficacy over other media is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils construct and interpret food chains and identify producers, predators and prey
Students model the movement of matter/energy among organisms via food webs

Antarctic food webs are underpinned by phytoplankton and Antarctic krill supporting fish, penguins, seals and whales; Arctic chains run from ice algae through zooplankton and fish to seals and polar bears
learnerActions: From a jumbled set of organism cards or on-screen tokens, place the producer first at the base — phytoplankton, marked with a little sun icon to show it is powered by sunlight.
Add krill, then a penguin, then a leopard seal, drawing or snapping an arrow between each pair.

Read each arrow aloud as 'is eaten by / energy flows to': 'phytoplankton is eaten by krill', 'krill is eaten by penguin', 'penguin is eaten by leopard seal'. If an arrow is pointing the wrong way, flip it so it points toward the eater.

Once the chain is complete, remove the krill and trace out loud what happens up this chain: the penguin runs short of food, then the leopard seal that eats penguins also goes hungry. (Real penguins and seals can eat some other foods, but krill are a major food for many Antarctic animals.)
State in your own words why the smallest organism can matter most to the whole chain.
activities.intendedInsight: In polar seas the tiniest producers and krill hold up the largest predators; arrows carry energy upward from the sunlit base, and losing a small link cascades all the way to the top.

activities.title: Compare the two poles side by side
feedback: If a learner thinks the poles have completely different food systems, line the two chains up and ask them to match each Antarctic link to the Arctic link that plays the same role.
If the producer is misidentified, ask which organism is powered by sunlight and sits at the base.
activities.rationale: Placing the two chains together surfaces the common structure and reinforces that each starts from a sunlight-powered producer. A side-by-side toggle is a helpful way to make the parallel visible but is not required.
sourceClaims: Antarctic food webs are underpinned by phytoplankton and Antarctic krill supporting fish, penguins, seals and whales; Arctic chains run from ice algae through zooplankton and fish to seals and polar bears
learnerActions: Build or lay out the Antarctic chain (phytoplankton → krill → penguin/fish → leopard seal/orca) and the Arctic chain (ice algae → zooplankton → fish → seal → polar bear) next to each other.
Toggle or point between them and name, for each, the producer, a consumer, and a top predator.
Describe the shared shape: producer → consumer → predator, with a tiny sunlight-powered organism at every base.
activities.intendedInsight: Both poles follow the same producer→consumer→predator pattern, so the two systems are parallel, not wholly different.

activities.title: Order-the-chain and arrow-direction check
feedback: If arrows are pointed from eater to food, restate that the arrow follows the energy to whoever does the eating.
If an animal is placed at the start, remind the learner that chains start with a sunlight-powered producer.
activities.rationale: Ordering and arrow-direction items are efficient for checking the sequence and the arrow convention. They verify these quickly but do not themselves elicit the remove-a-link cascade reasoning, so they best accompany the build-and-perturb task rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils construct and interpret food chains and identify producers, predators and prey
learnerActions: Given a scrambled set of polar organisms, arrange them in order from producer to top predator.
Choose which way each arrow should point and justify it using the 'is eaten by / energy flows to' rule.
Answer: at the very start of a polar food chain, what kind of organism is it, and why does something so tiny matter so much?
activities.intendedInsight: Sequence and arrow direction can be checked quickly, consolidating the vocabulary of producer, consumer and predator.

activities.title: Interview a krill (spoken hook)
feedback: If the interview turns the krill into a top predator, remind the learner the krill eats the phytoplankton and is itself eaten by penguins and fish.
Encourage the learner to check each claim from the interview against the chain they build.
activities.rationale: A conversation is an engaging hook for the big idea but does not itself let the learner construct or perturb the chain; it is best used to set up the hands-on building activity, not to carry the core learning alone.
learnerActions: Role-play a short interview with a krill 'holding up the whole Antarctic', asking who depends on it and what would happen if it vanished.
Have the krill explain where it gets its own energy (eating phytoplankton, which is powered by the sun).
After the hook, move to building and perturbing a real chain to test the claims made in the interview.
activities.intendedInsight: A playful voice can motivate the idea that the smallest organism supports the whole web, before the learner tests it by construction.

constraints: Teach the arrow explicitly and repeatedly as 'is eaten by / energy flows to' — it points toward the eater; reversing it is the classic error.
Every polar chain must start at a sunlight-powered producer (phytoplankton or ice algae), never at an animal.
Make the tiny producers and krill central: they support the largest predators, so the base is not the least important part.
Order and arrow-direction items check the sequence and the arrow convention but do not themselves elicit the remove-a-link cascade reasoning; pair them with an actual build-and-perturb task.
The conversational krill interview is a motivating hook, not a substitute for constructing and perturbing a chain.
A tap-to-reveal labelled chain teaches sequence and vocabulary but cannot by itself deliver the remove-a-link cascade; treat it as a scaffold toward hands-on construction.
Food-chain reasoning is relational rather than spatial, so a spatial/3D depiction is not required for this objective (this is a scoped observation, not a claim that 3D could add nothing in general).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all three sources remain unverified (verified:false) in the original row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a 3D treatment 'poor' asserting it 'adds no explanatory value'; softened here to a scoped observation that this relational objective does not require spatial depiction, rather than a universal modality claim.

The original framed a drag-builder as doing 'exactly what a static list cannot'; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the cited sources, so activity 1's rationale now uses intended wording and leaves efficacy open.
Energy-pyramid wording ('many tiny krill support few big predators') is a simplification; kept as a hint about numbers/importance, not presented as a quantified law.

The original assessment's 'partial' response band (reads arrows OR knows the base, not both) was not needed as learner-facing text and is recorded in the preservation audit rather than reproduced here.

probeDeeper: Read the chain aloud using the arrow to mean 'is eaten by'. Does 'krill is eaten by penguin' make sense that way?
What is at the very START of a polar food chain, and why is something so tiny so important?
If the krill vanished, walk me up the chain — who runs short of food, step by step?
Is the biggest animal or the smallest the one the whole chain most depends on? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: The arrows point from the food to the EATER — they show the direction energy flows (phytoplankton are eaten BY krill, krill BY penguins, penguins BY leopard seals), so the arrow points toward whoever does the eating, not toward the prey. And the tiny organisms at the START (phytoplankton and krill) are the foundation of everything: if the krill vanished, the penguins would lose their main food and crash, and the leopard seals and orcas above them would starve too. The smallest creatures, not the biggest, hold the whole chain up.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Food-chain arrows point to the prey / to what gets eaten' — reverses the energy-flow convention.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix the rule: the arrow means 'is eaten by' / 'energy goes to' — it points to the EATER. Re-read the chain aloud with that rule.
errorPatterns.distractor: The arrows point from each animal to the food it eats.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads 'krill → penguin' as 'krill eats penguin', or points arrows toward the food.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The biggest predator is the most important' — undervalues the tiny base.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Flip the pyramid's importance: the tiny plankton and krill feed everything above; remove them and the whole chain falls.
errorPatterns.distractor: The leopard seal matters most because it's the biggest animal in the chain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the leopard seal/orca as most important; overlooks plankton and krill.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Removing the krill only affects the krill' — no sense of knock-on effects up the chain.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the ripple: fewer krill → fewer penguins → fewer leopard seals; the loss travels all the way up.
errorPatterns.distractor: If the krill disappeared, only the krill would be affected — nothing else.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says only krill numbers change; doesn't follow the effect up to penguins and seals.

responseLevels.gap: Reverses the arrows and thinks the biggest predator is most important.
responseLevels.full: Reads arrows as energy flowing to the eater, identifies phytoplankton/krill as the foundation, and traces how losing the krill starves penguins and then leopard seals — transferring the reasoning to the Arctic chain too.
responseLevels.partial: Reads arrows correctly OR knows plankton/krill are the base, but not both, or can't trace the effect of removing the krill upward.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is an Antarctic food chain shown with arrows: phytoplankton → krill → penguin → leopard seal. A student reads it as 'the leopard seal is the most important because it's biggest, and the arrows show who eats who — pointing from the eater to its food.' Which way do the arrows really point, and if all the tiny krill vanished, what would happen to the seals and penguins — why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student with the two documented errors reverses the arrows and thinks the biggest predator matters most; a student with the concept reads arrows as energy-to-the-eater and identifies krill/plankton as the load-bearing base whose loss collapses the chain. Both the arrow-direction and the 'remove the krill' questions expose the misconceptions cleanly.
